demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again
I remind myself it could have been worse
I dwell on what I have done wrong

Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I feel isolated and set apart from others
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm as a coping strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only markedly high-risk/impulsive strategy and is poorly supported by the rest of the selected nodes. The other strategies are comparatively cognitive/obsessional (mental rituals, downward comparison), and the threat/memory/appraisal items do not show the broader dysregulation, dissociation, or severe affective overload that would make this combination clinically cohesive.

issues.item: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Pain recall implies the patient was physically injured in the traumatic event. That is hard to reconcile with the trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another' unless she was also injured, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. The rest of the memory items emphasize fragmented retrieval and sensory reliving, but not a personally injured trauma narrative.

vignette: The incident occurred on a Thursday during a routine walkthrough of the downtown renovation site. Amara was inspecting the tension cables on the third-floor atrium when her grip slipped on the heavy torque wrench. She had braced herself to steady it, but the momentum carried the tool backward, striking her knee and sending her stumbling into a temporary railing. The railing gave way, and a suspended steel plank, loosened by the shift, dropped onto the foreman’s shin. The sound of the impact—a sharp, ringing fracture followed by the groan of bending metal—still surfaced in her mind unbidden. She could taste the coppery tang of her own bitten lip and the fine grit of the construction floor when the memory returns, carried on the same breath as the event. In the weeks that followed, ordinary moments began to feel charged. A dropped manila folder in the firm’s reception area made her jump as if a load might follow it down. She reacted to the clatter of the breakroom microwave, the hiss of the espresso machine, and the sudden slam of an office door as though each carried the same latent threat. She had come to believe that danger was always hovering just beyond the periphery, waiting for a misstep. When she tried to deliberately trace the sequence of events from that afternoon, she often found her mind slipping, unable to access the full picture. Instead, fragments surfaced: the screech of the cable, the foreman’s sharp intake of breath, the exact angle of the falling plank. She would catch herself hearing those sounds in her head, layered over the present, making the drafting table feel like the construction site all over again. To keep the unsettling from returning, Amara began performing quiet mental rituals. Before opening a heavy door, she would silently count her breaths, convinced that maintaining a steady rhythm would keep the world steady. At home, she reminded herself that the foreman had recovered, that hospital records showed no permanent damage, and that far worse outcomes were possible. Yet the thoughts of what she had done wrong anchored her attention. She replayed the moment her fingers lost purchase, the split second she had misjudged the railing’s weight, wondering if a different grip or a slower turn would have changed everything. Her husband noticed the shift. He saw her withdraw from evening conversations, her eyes fixed on some internal calculation, and felt the quiet distance growing between them. She was not ill, she insisted, but she was no longer the woman who could walk onto a site without looking up. Months later, the habits hardened. Amara avoided site visits when possible, delegating walkthroughs to junior staff. When she did attend, she stood at the perimeter, her shoulders slightly hunched, monitoring the space as though it might tip at any moment. Her concentration frayed during detailed drafting sessions; she would lose her place on a blueprint, the lines blurring together until she had to step back and start again. She had come to believe that someone else would not have slipped, would not have caused such a disruption, and that her own presence felt too large for the rooms she occupied. Colleagues noticed her hesitation in meetings, her careful word choice, and the way she kept her distance from the more boisterous project leads. She felt set apart, watching the firm’s usual rhythm while she moved through it like a ghost. Her own reflection felt unfamiliar. The confident architect who once directed site crews with a calm authority now navigated her daily life as though walking on a suspended scaffold. What frightened her most was not a recurrence of the injury, but the quiet erosion of her routine certainty. She had come to seek help, as the mental rituals, the startle responses, and the relentless replay of a single afternoon began to constrain her work and her marriage. She hoped to reclaim the woman who could look at a blueprint without searching for hidden loads, and to stop waiting for the world to fall again.
